newsitem.title: USA: U.S. House passes $20 billion energy spending bill.
newsitem.headline: U.S. House passes $20 billion energy spending bill.

text.p: The U.S. House of Representatives approved a $20 billion spending bill for energy and water programs for the 1997 fiscal year, and the White House said it expected President Clinton would sign it.
The compromise House-Senate bill, which passed the House on a vote of 383-29, provided $700 million more than last year, but $200 million less than the administration requested.
Half the funding was devoted to the Energy Department's nuclear weapons activities and nuclear waste cleanup.

The final bill allotted $3.9 billion for nuclear weapons management, including weapons storage and scientific testing, and $5.45 billion for cleanup of radioactive waste left from 50 years of weapons manufacturing.
Administration officials said the bill was acceptable. "We think that generally the committee has done a very fine job and we support the bill," said Deputy Energy Secretary Charles Curtis.
"The conferees noticeably took into account at least some of our major concerns," said a spokesman for the White House Office of Management and Budget.
Congress dropped a provision that potentially would have cut off funding for studies on a site in Nevada for a long-delayed nuclear waste dump.
It also dropped language specifying sharp cuts in staff levels in the Energy Secretary's office, although the bill trimmed spending on departmental administration.
The administration bowed to lawmakers' agreement to allot $270 million for solar and renewable energy research, $90 million less than they requested, but $23 million more than first proposed.

"We're disappointed with the disposal of the solar and renewables budget which is something that this administration has placed a high priority on, but has been unable to convince the Congress to make the investment in," Curtis said.

Lawmakers agreed to provide $38 million to continue research on an advanced light water nuclear reactor, which a coalition of conservative think tanks and anti-nuclear groups said was unnecessary because utilities do not plan to build more nuclear reactors.

The bill funded Army Corps of Engineers projects at $1.1 billion, $277 million more than last year, including $9 million to begin construction on the controversial Animas-La Plata water project in Colorado.
The project is expected to eventually cost more than $700 million, with Washington to foot more than half the bill. Critics say the project will generate only 36 cents for every federal dollar spent.
